slides.heading: Disk Stacking
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Hard · Dynamic Programming
slides.narration: Let's solve Disk Stacking, a hard dynamic programming problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Disks [width, depth, height]; stack them so each disk is strictly smaller in all three dimensions than the one below, maximising total height.
Returns the chosen disks ordered from top (smallest) to bottom (largest).
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Disks width, depth, height ; stack them so each disk is strictly smaller in all three dimensions than the one below, maximising total height. Returns the chosen disks ordered from top (smallest) to bottom (largest).

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Sort disks by height; each disk's best stack is itself on top of the best compatible stack below.
slides.narration: Sort disks by height; each disk's best stack is itself on top of the best compatible stack below.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Sort by height, LIS-style DP → O(n²)
slides.narration: Trying every order is exponential. Sorting by height and running a longest-increasing-subsequence style DP over strictly smaller disks is quadratic.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 2. For each disk, check smaller earlier disks
3. Keep the best height and a predecessor link
slides.narration: Step by step. First, sort by height. Second, for each disk, check smaller earlier disks. Third, keep the best height and a predecessor link. Fourth, rebuild the stack.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We sort by height. For each disk, start with its own height, and for each earlier strictly smaller disk extend if taller. Track the best index, then follow prev to build the answer.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n squared. Space is O of n.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Sorting by one dimension is enough
slides.narration: All three dimensions must be strictly smaller.
